objectives: Find the limiting resource from a per-operation demand model.
Calculate headroom with explicit utilization and failure assumptions.
Perform sensitivity analysis on uncertain inputs.
Compare operating cost without treating illustrative prices as current quotes.
retrieval: From L007: how long does a backlog take to drain when new work still arrives?
From L006: distinguish live data and provisioned capacity.

sections.title: A pipeline is limited by its tightest relevant resource
sections.markdown:
Core budget: retrieval 5, explanation 18, worked decision 8, exercise 10, questions 10, review 4 minutes. A campus image converter accepts a picture and returns a thumbnail. Assume each request consumes 20 ms of CPU, reads 1 MB, writes 100 kB, and has a 500 ms interactive deadline. These costs are supplied teaching measurements; they do not describe your computer or a cloud instance.

An eight-core machine has at most eight CPU-seconds available per wall-clock second. At 0.020 CPU-seconds/request, the ideal CPU bound is 400 requests/s. This is a resource-accounting upper bound, not a safe benchmark result. It ignores scheduling overhead, other processes, uneven task sizes, and contention. If you target at most 60% CPU use under the representative peak, the planning CPU capacity becomes 240 requests/s.

Suppose effective storage read capacity is 150 MB/s. At 1 MB/read per request it bounds demand at 150 requests/s, below the CPU planning value. More CPU alone cannot fix that read bottleneck. Reducing read bytes, improving the storage path, or exploiting valid reuse might. The requirement and access pattern choose the remedy.

Some resources are counts rather than rates: maximum open connections, memory for concurrent work, or available identifiers. Check them using the right model. A service may fit average disk bandwidth but exhaust memory during a slow dependency, as L007 showed.

sections.title: State exactly which bad day you are reserving for
sections.markdown:
Headroom is spare capacity relative to an explicit scenario. It may cover workload uncertainty, burstiness, recovery, or a failed instance. If one machine safely sustains 100 requests/s at the required latency and peak demand is 180/s, two machines provide only 20/s spare while both are healthy. Losing one leaves half the fleet and too little capacity. Three such machines provide 200/s with one lost, assuming balanced routing and no shared bottleneck.

For identical independent instances, a simple one-failure sizing rule is n ≥ ceil(peak / sustainable_capacity_per_instance) + 1. It only applies if the measured per-instance capacity remains valid together, failover works, data dependencies still fit, and the failure does not remove more than one instance. Two copies on the same host do not satisfy a host-failure assumption.

Avoid hiding every uncertainty in one multiplier. A peak factor describes demand shape. A target utilization describes operating margin. A failure reserve describes lost capacity. They can all be appropriate, but each should have a purpose so you can detect double counting. Do not multiply peak demand by two “for safety” and then also require 50% utilization without explaining whether those cover distinct risks.

Spare capacity is not instantaneous recovery. Detection, rerouting, warm-up, and data loading take time. A design can have enough theoretical surviving capacity while violating latency during the transition.

sections.title: A small table can change the architecture
sections.markdown:
For the image converter, evaluate three input-size scenarios:

| Average source bytes | Read bound at 150 MB/s | Consequence |
|---|---:|---|
| 0.5 MB | 300 requests/s | CPU planning bound of 240/s dominates |
| 1 MB | 150 requests/s | Storage reads dominate |
| 3 MB | 50 requests/s | Storage dominates much earlier |

This table identifies a useful next measurement: source-image size and effective read throughput. It also prevents an expensive response to the wrong bottleneck. Buying more CPU while images triple in size does not follow from the model.

Now compare two hypothetical plans. Plan A costs 100 cost-units/month per machine and needs three machines. Plan B costs 180 per machine, sustains twice the tested rate, and needs two machines for the same one-failure scenario. Machine cost is 300 versus 360 units. But Plan B may reduce patching or coordination work; Plan A may offer a smaller failure increment. These are invented cost units, not cloud price quotes. Add storage, network transfer, backups, and operator effort before choosing.

Arithmetic implementation, executable with Python 3.11+:

~~~python
from math import ceil

def instances(peak_rps: float, safe_rps: float, failed: int = 1) -> int:
    assert peak_rps >= 0 and safe_rps > 0 and failed >= 0
    return ceil(peak_rps / safe_rps) + failed

assert instances(180, 100) == 3
assert instances(180, 200) == 2
print("A: 3 instances; B: 2 instances")
~~~

The function validates a sizing formula, not routing behavior or real-world service capacity.

sections.title: Scaling evidence must include the shared dependency
sections.markdown:
Suppose each application copy individually reaches 100/s, but all copies share a database capped at 150 useful operations/s. Three copies do not produce 300/s. Parallelism increases pressure on the same authority. Benchmarking one copy then multiplying by fleet size is a hypothesis to test, not demonstrated scalability.

A failure can also change request cost. If cached thumbnails disappear, each request may read and convert the original image. A replica recovering from disk can compete with foreground reads. Capacity planning should therefore name degraded modes, not only the happy-path peak.

Common misconceptions include “70% CPU is always safe,” “autoscaling has no delay,” “a larger machine fixes every bottleneck,” “cost equals the server bill,” and “twice the components means twice the capacity.” The correction is not another universal percentage; it is a demand-per-resource model with measured sustainable limits and failure assumptions.

Finish a capacity argument in three sentences: identify the limiting resource under the current model; state the amount of margin and the event it covers; name the measurement or requirement change that would make you revisit the design. Optional depth is a real benchmark on your machine, explicitly separate from the supplied illustrative measurements.

exercise.prompt: A service peaks at 260 requests/s. A representative benchmark shows one instance sustaining 100/s at the required latency, but its shared database sustains only 220/s. Explain why adding a fourth application instance alone does not meet the requirement. Give a one-instance-loss sizing calculation after the database is improved to 500/s. Identify one remaining failure assumption.
rubric: Identifies shared database as the current bottleneck.
Does not sum app capacity past the shared limit.
Calculates three survivors plus one failure reserve.
Names routing, correlated failure, or degraded-cost assumptions.
exercise.solution: At 260/s demand, the 220/s shared database saturates regardless of a fourth application copy. Improve or reduce database demand and verify its 500/s limit under the actual mix. After that, ceil(260/100)+1 = 4 application instances covers loss of one, leaving nominal 300/s. This assumes traffic reaches survivors, capacities are sustainable together, and the lost failure domain contains only one copy. Database failure tolerance remains a separate question.

questions.prompt: 4 CPU cores, 10 ms CPU/request: ideal CPU-only upper bound?
A shared dependency caps useful throughput at 200/s. Adding app replicas necessarily:
options: May increase pressure without lifting the shared limit
questions.answer: May increase pressure without lifting the shared limit
questions.explanation: The bottleneck remains shared unless its workload or capacity changes.

questions.prompt: Peak 350/s, sustainable instance rate 100/s, reserve for one lost instance. How many instances?
Why state the purpose of each headroom factor?
questions.answer: To separate peak shape, utilization margin, failure reserve, and uncertainty so the same risk is not counted twice or omitted.
questions.explanation: A factor with no scenario is hard to validate or revise.

questions.prompt: When would the cheaper server plan be more expensive overall?
questions.answer: When it adds enough operator work, network or storage charges, failure exposure, or migration burden to exceed the apparent machine saving.
questions.explanation: Use explicit assumptions and comparable scopes, not invented current prices.

flashcards.back: That fleet capacity is automatically the sum of isolated instance benchmarks.
